clinicalPearls: Slowly progressive, often adult-onset cerebellar ataxia caused by a combined CTG-CAG repeat expansion at the ATXN8/ATXN8OS locus

The locus is transcribed bidirectionally, producing both a non-coding CTG (ATXN8OS) transcript and a CAG (ATXN8) polyglutamine transcript, so it shares features of both toxic RNA and polyglutamine mechanisms
Marked reduced penetrance and variable expansion size complicate interpretation, so a positive result must be correlated with the clinical picture
Typical features include gait and limb ataxia, scanning dysarthria, nystagmus and variable spasticity
Onset is usually in adulthood but ranges widely, and progression is generally slow
MRI shows cerebellar atrophy, sometimes with pontine involvement
Because expanded alleles occur in unaffected individuals, the test alone does not confirm symptomatic disease
Management is supportive with physiotherapy, speech therapy and falls prevention
reference.pathophysiology: SCA8 arises from an unstable combined CTG-CAG repeat expansion at the ATXN8OS/ATXN8 locus. The region is bidirectionally transcribed: the ATXN8OS strand yields a CUG-containing non-coding RNA thought to exert an RNA toxic gain-of-function similar to the myotonic dystrophies, while the opposite ATXN8 strand encodes a nearly pure polyglutamine protein via a CAG expansion. Both mechanisms are implicated in Purkinje cell and cerebellar degeneration. The considerable variability in expansion length, incomplete penetrance and presence of expanded alleles in the general population make genotype-phenotype correlation less clear-cut than in other repeat ataxias.
additionalDifferentials: Other autosomal dominant spinocerebellar ataxias (SCA1, SCA2, SCA3, SCA6)
Myotonic dystrophy and other RNA repeat-expansion disorders
additionalInvestigations: Targeted ATXN8/ATXN8OS CTG-CAG repeat analysis interpreted alongside the clinical picture
Broad spinocerebellar ataxia repeat-expansion panel to exclude other subtypes
MRI brain to document cerebellar and any brainstem atrophy
Nerve conduction studies to assess for associated neuropathy
Screening for acquired causes (vitamin, thyroid, autoimmune, paraneoplastic)
Family history review and consideration of genetic counselling given reduced penetrance
redFlags: Rapid or subacute progression suggesting an acquired rather than genetic cause
Prominent autonomic failure raising the possibility of multiple system atrophy
Systemic myotonia or cardiac features prompting reassessment for myotonic dystrophy
A positive repeat result in a minimally symptomatic person that risks over-diagnosis
reference.prognosis: SCA8 usually follows a slowly progressive course over years to decades with generally preserved life expectancy, though disability from gait ataxia and dysarthria accumulates over time. Reduced penetrance means some expansion carriers remain mildly affected or asymptomatic.
pitfalls: Treating a positive expansion as definitive proof of disease despite the locus's reduced penetrance
Failing to exclude treatable acquired ataxias before attributing symptoms to SCA8
Overlooking myotonic dystrophy given the shared RNA toxicity mechanism
Providing overly deterministic genetic counselling without acknowledging variable expressivity
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying therapy; symptomatic and supportive management of the cerebellar syndrome
Physiotherapy with balance and gait training, and occupational therapy for aids and fall prevention
Speech and language therapy for scanning dysarthria, with swallow assessment for dysphagia
Symptomatic treatment of nystagmus and oscillopsia, and antispasticity agents where spasticity is troublesome
Periodic neurological review to monitor progression and safety
Genetic counselling that explicitly addresses reduced penetrance and variable expansion size when advising relatives
Referral to specialist ataxia services and patient support networks
